turns.prompt_text: I'd like to make a little automatic fish feeder for a small ponds I'm sure they already exist but so many people still do them manually because of how expensive they are And my natural intuition is that this is easily solvable for much less than what they are asking My naive approach was to have some kind of water gal in her large tank feeding into an auger that will then feed into some kind of Nerf vector blaster that shoots those little Nerf balls and just duct taping around the shooter cylinders so that they become a narrower firing area This would in total three DC motors The timing circuit would be relatively simple It could be something more dedicated or just something that starts whenever the sun rises and just happens some number of times a day at some interval until it runs out of energy I'm thinking of using either lithium ion batteries or just straight capacitors because of how much sun we have here
turns.response_html:
Your intuition is spot on: commercial pond feeders are wildly marked up for what is essentially a basic material-handling problem. You can absolutely build this for a fraction of the cost, and your breakdown of the mechanical stages is incredibly solid.

Let's break down your naive approach, look at where it works, where it might jam, and how to optimize it for simplicity, reliability, and power.

1. The Mechanical Flight Path

Using an auger to meter out the food is the gold standard for automated feeding. However, the "Nerf blaster" stage might introduce unnecessary complexity and point-of-failure risks (jamming, crushed pellets, high current spikes).

Instead, we can borrow a trick from commercial feeders and agricultural spreaders: The Slotted Slinger Disk.

[ Large Hopper / Tank ]
          │ (Gravity feed)
          ▼
   [ Motor 1: Auger ]  <-- Measures precise amount of food
          │ (Drops pellets down)
          ▼
[ Motor 2: Slinger Disk ] <-- High-speed spinning plate with fins
          │
          └──► [ Blasts pellets outward across the pond ]

Why a Slinger over a Vector Blaster?

  • Lower Motor Count: This drops your design from 3 DC motors down to 2 DC motors (one for the auger, one for the slinger).
  • Zero Jamming: Pellets drop onto a spinning plate with vertical fins/walls. Centrifugal force flings them out of a directional chute. It won't jam if pellets bunch up, whereas flywheels/compressors require precise, single-file feeding.
  • Variable Range: You can control how far the food shoots simply by adjusting the voltage (and thus the speed) of the slinger motor.

2. Power: Lithium-Ion vs. Supercapacitors

Because you have abundant sunlight, a solar-charged system is perfect. However, capacitors alone likely won't cut it here.

  • The Verdict: Go with a Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) or Lithium-ion battery paired with a small solar panel.
  • Why Caps Fall Short: High-RPM DC motors (especially if you stick with a flywheel/blaster concept) pull significant starting current. Supercapacitors drop voltage linearly as they discharge. A few seconds of spinning a motor will tank the voltage below what your timing circuit needs to run stably.
  • The Sweet Spot: A cheap 12V 7Ah LiFePO4 battery (or even a few 18650 cells in series) handles high current spikes effortlessly, charges safely in the sun via a cheap solar charge controller, and will easily last through a week of heavy overcast days.

3. The Control Circuit: Keep it Simple

You mentioned a simple timing circuit. Depending on how much you want to build vs. buy, you have two great paths:

Path A: The "Zero Code" Hardware Route

You can use a Digital Cycle Timer Relay (like a dual-timer XY-LJ02 or similar generic modules found online for under $10).

  • You can configure it to trigger every $X$ hours, turn on the slinger motor first, delay a second, turn on the auger motor for 5 seconds to drop food, turn off the auger, and then turn off the slinger.

Path B: The Microcontroller Route (Recommended for Solar)

An ESP32 or Arduino Nano paired with a cheap RTC (Real-Time Clock) module gives you flawless execution.

  • The "Sun Rise" Method: You can use a simple photoresistor (LDR) to detect dawn. When light hits a certain threshold, the microcontroller wakes up from a low-power deep sleep mode, runs the feeding sequence, and goes back to sleep.
  • Deep Sleep is Key: By keeping the microcontroller in deep sleep between feeds, your idle power draw drops to microamps, making your solar/battery footprint incredibly small.

4. Engineering Headaches to Avoid

Before you start printing or cutting materials, keep these physical constraints in mind:

  • Humidity & Condensation: This is the killer of all automatic feeders. Fish food is highly hygroscopic (it loves absorbing water). If pond mist or humidity gets up into the auger tube, the pellets will turn into a doughy paste and lock up the motor. Ensure your slinger/output chute points downward and has a physical lip or shield to block rising vapor.
  • Auger Tolerances: If you 3D print the auger, ensure the clearance between the auger blade and the tube wall is either smaller than your smallest fish pellet, or significantly larger. If the clearance matches the pellet size, the pellets will lodge between the blade and the wall, drawing massive current and stalling the motor.

How large is the pond you are trying to cover? That will dictate how fast that slinger motor needs to spin to get the coverage you need.

turns.prompt_text: Very nice. This is definitely doable. We could use some kind of battery pack that gets charged up by the solar panel and is then used up during the feeding and then charge the rest of the day for the next morning run The distance depends on the pond so it could vary but generally I think between 4 ft and 20 ft These fish food pellets are small. No bigger and half a cm in diameter
turns.response_html:
That distance is highly achievable with a slinger design. Throwing light, half-centimeter pellets up to 20 feet is all about tip velocity—the speed at which the outer edge of your spinning disk transfers kinetic energy to the pellet.

With a battery-backed solar setup, you'll have plenty of instantaneous current to drive the motor fast enough to reach that 20-foot mark.

Here is how you can dial in the mechanics, the power budget, and the trajectory to hit that exact distance range.

1. Calculating the Slinger Metrics

To get a 20-foot ($~6\text{ meters}$) throw with small pellets, your slinger disk needs to spin fast enough to overcome air resistance.

The Disk Design

  • Diameter: A 4-inch ($10\text{ cm}$) diameter disk is a sweet spot for 3D printing or cutting from scrap plastic. It’s large enough to give the pellets a good ride outward but small enough not to overload a small motor.
  • The Geometry: Print or cut a flat disk with 2 to 4 vertical ribs (fins) radiating outward from the center. These fins push the pellets, forcing them to match the rotational speed of the disk before they fly off the edge.

Motor Selection

To hit 20 feet, look for a standard 12V DC motor rated for roughly 3,000 to 5,000 RPM (unloaded).

  • By using a simple PWM motor speed controller (a $5 dial module), you can manually adjust the motor's speed. Crank it up for a 20-ft pond, or dial it back to low voltage if you only need a 4-ft toss.

2. Solar & Battery Budgeting

Your strategy of charging all day for a high-energy morning run is incredibly efficient. Because the motors only run for a few seconds per day, your total daily amp-hour consumption is shockingly low.

Let's look at the math for a standard feeding cycle:

  • Slinger Motor: ~2 Amps active draw for 10 seconds.
  • Auger Motor: ~1 Amp active draw for 5 seconds.

$$\text{Total energy per feed} \approx (2\text{A} \times 10\text{s}) + (1\text{A} \times 5\text{s}) = 25\text{ Amp-seconds}$$

Since $1\text{ Ah} = 3,600\text{ Amp-seconds}$, a single feeding uses less than 0.007 Ah.

Even a tiny 12V 1.2Ah or 3Ah LiFePO4 battery gives you massive headroom and can easily handle the 2-Amp surge current. A small 5W to 10W solar panel paired with a basic solar regulator will fully replenish that daily energy use in less than an hour of morning sunlight, leaving the rest of the day to keep the battery topped off and healthy.

3. Optimizing the Trajectory Chute

To get the food out to 20 feet instead of just spraying it in a chaotic 360-degree circle, you'll want to house the slinger disk inside a directional shroud.

       [ Auger Drops Food Here ]
                 │
                 ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────┐
    │     / / / / / / /       │  <-- Enclosed Shroud
    │    /  Spinning   \      │
    │   |     Disk     |      │
    └───┼─             ───────┘
        │             /
        └────────────/   <--- Open Directed Chute (angled 30-45°)
                      \
                       └──► [ Pellets launch toward pond ]
  • The Angle: The exit chute should point upward at roughly a $30^\circ$ to $45^\circ$ angle. This utilizes the physics of projectile motion to maximize your horizontal distance. If it shoots completely flat, gravity drops the light pellets into the water too early.
  • The Feed Timing Trick: Always program the circuit to turn the slinger motor on 2 seconds before the auger starts spinning. This ensures the disk is already at max RPM when the first $0.5\text{ cm}$ pellets drop onto it, preventing a pile-up that could choke the motor or drop food directly beneath the feeder.

Are you planning to mount this on a post at the edge of the pond, or will it be sitting flat on a dock? The mounting height will give you some free extra distance on the throw.
